entries.title: Chelete Credit Limited v Office of the Data Protection Commissioner & Another
entries.principle: Enforcement notices issued by the Commissioner must be proportionate and reasoned; a controller may challenge both the finding and the remedy on appeal.

entries.title: Maingi v Nairobi Java House Ltd
entries.principle: The collection and use of personal data by a private entity must be proportionate to the purpose and subject to the Act's safeguards.

entries.title: Odhiambo v Manpower Networks Ltd
entries.court: Employment and Labour Relations Court of Kenya
entries.principle: Employee personal data must be processed lawfully and fairly; monitoring and use of such data must be proportionate to a legitimate employment purpose.

entries.title: Platinum Credit Limited v Office of the Data Protection Commissioner & Another
entries.principle: The Commissioner's powers of investigation and enforcement are broad but must be exercised in accordance with the Act and the rules of natural justice.

entries.title: WPP Scangroup PLC & Another v Data Commissioner & 2 Others
entries.principle: Cross-border transfers and the use of personal data in commercial profiling must be assessed against the Act's principles of lawful basis, transparency and minimisation.

entries.title: Arunda v Office of the Data Protection Commissioner & Another
entries.principle: The Data Protection Commissioner's decisions are subject to judicial review; data subjects have the right to seek redress for violations of their privacy and data protection rights.
entries.facts: A challenge to the Data Protection Commissioner's decision. The petitioner alleged violations of privacy and data protection rights. The case raised questions of the Commissioner's jurisdiction and remedies.
entries.holding: The Court held that the Commissioner's decisions are subject to judicial review and that data subjects have the right to seek redress for violations of their privacy rights.

entries.title: Katiba Institute v Parliament of the Republic of Kenya & Another
entries.principle: Registration and processing of personal data for public purposes must satisfy the Data Protection Act, including transparency, purpose limitation and adequate safeguards against function creep.

entries.title: Opati v Safaricom PLC
entries.principle: A data controller that processes personal data without a lawful basis or adequate security may be liable in damages to the data subject.

entries.title: Regus Kenya Limited v Data Protection Commissioner & Another
entries.principle: The Data Protection Commissioner's jurisdiction and enforcement powers are subject to appeal; the Act's remedies must be interpreted purposively to protect data subjects.

entries.title: Republic v Tools for Humanity Corporation (US) & 9 Others; Katiba Institute & 4 Others (Ex parte Applicants)
entries.principle: Judicial review lies against the data regulator where its decisions on cross-border transfers and biometric processing are unlawful, irrational or procedurally unfair.

entries.title: Wambui & Another v Eden Park Country Garden Limited
entries.principle: The right to privacy protects personal information in commercial and property transactions; unlawful surveillance or disclosure violates Article 31.
entries.facts: A dispute concerning the unlawful collection and use of personal information in a property transaction. The petitioners alleged violations of privacy rights. The case raised questions of data protection in commercial contexts.
entries.holding: The Court held that the right to privacy under Article 31 protects personal information in commercial transactions; unlawful collection or use violates the Constitution.

entries.title: Kaibos v Ngawa 2019 Assets Limited
entries.principle: The right to privacy protects personal information and communications; unlawful surveillance or disclosure of private information violates Article 31.
entries.facts: A dispute concerning the unlawful disclosure and use of personal information. The petitioner alleged violations of privacy rights. The case raised questions of data protection and confidentiality.
entries.holding: The Court held that the right to privacy under Article 31 protects personal information; unlawful disclosure or misuse of personal data violates the Constitution.

entries.title: Office of the Data Protection Commissioner v Tools for Humanity Corporation (Worldcoin) & 2 others
entries.citation: [2024] KEHC 312 (KLR) (25 January 2024) (Miscellaneous Criminal Application E315 of 2023)
entries.principle: Processing of biometric and financial data must satisfy the Data Protection Act's lawful-basis, transparency, security and transfer safeguards; the Commissioner may take enforcement action where the controller has not demonstrated compliance.
entries.facts: The Office of the Data Protection Commissioner sought enforcement orders against Tools for Humanity (Worldcoin) for biometric data collection. The respondent had collected iris scans and financial data from Kenyan residents. The case raised questions of lawful basis, transparency, security and cross-border transfers under the Data Protection Act.
entries.holding: Processing of biometric and financial data must satisfy the Data Protection Act's lawful-basis, transparency, security and transfer safeguards; the Commissioner may take enforcement action where the controller has not demonstrated compliance.

entries.title: Phoro v Eldoret Technical Training Institute
entries.principle: The right to privacy protects personal information held by public institutions; unlawful disclosure or misuse of personal data violates Article 31.
entries.facts: A challenge to the handling of personal data by a public training institution. The petitioner alleged violations of privacy rights. The case raised questions of data protection in public institutions.
entries.holding: The Court held that the right to privacy under Article 31 protects personal information held by public institutions; unlawful disclosure or misuse violates the Constitution.

entries.title: Okeyo v Diamond Trust Bank (K) Ltd (Cause 1 of 2019)
entries.court: Employment and Labour Relations Court of Kenya
entries.principle: Employee personal data and workplace monitoring must be proportionate to a legitimate employment purpose; unfair termination attracts compensation.

entries.title: Ondieki v Maeda (Petition E153 of 2022)
entries.principle: The right to privacy protects personal and family life; interference must be lawful, necessary and proportionate.
entries.facts: A dispute concerning the violation of privacy rights. The petitioner alleged unlawful interference with personal and family life. The case raised questions of Article 31 and the limits of privacy.
entries.holding: The Court held that the right to privacy under Article 31 protects personal and family life; any interference must be lawful, necessary and proportionate.

entries.title: ZXC v Bloomberg LP
entries.court: Supreme Court of the United Kingdom
entries.principle: A person under criminal investigation has, in general, a reasonable expectation of privacy in information about that investigation before charge, subject to the fact-specific balancing exercise.
entries.facts: Bloomberg published an article naming a businessman under criminal investigation before charge.
entries.holding: A person under criminal investigation has, in general, a reasonable expectation of privacy in information about that investigation before charge.

entries.title: Big Brother Watch and Others v United Kingdom
entries.court: European Court of Human Rights (Grand Chamber)
entries.principle: Bulk interception regimes must contain sufficient safeguards against abuse, including independent authorisation and oversight, to be compatible with Article 8.

entries.title: Lloyd v Google LLC
entries.court: Supreme Court of the United Kingdom
entries.principle: A claim for damages under data protection law requires proof of material damage or distress; loss of control of data alone is insufficient.
entries.facts: A claim for damages for loss of control of personal data by Google.
entries.holding: A claim for damages under data protection law requires proof of material damage or distress; loss of control of data alone is insufficient.

entries.title: Privacy International v Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs
entries.court: Court of Justice of the European Union
entries.principle: National legislation requiring providers to retain traffic data for security purposes must comply with Union law; general retention is incompatible with fundamental rights.
entries.facts: A challenge to UK legislation requiring providers to retain communications data.
entries.holding: National legislation requiring providers to retain traffic data for security purposes must comply with Union law; general retention is incompatible with fundamental rights.
entries.judges: Court of Justice of the European Union

entries.title: Republic v Fred Matiang'i, Cabinet Secretary, Ministry of Interior & 3 Others; Katiba Institute & Another (Interested Parties)
entries.principle: A national biometric and digital identity programme requires a statutory basis, a data protection impact assessment and public participation before rollout.

entries.title: Data Protection Commissioner v Facebook Ireland Limited and Maximillian Schrems
entries.court: Court of Justice of the European Union
entries.principle: Transfers of personal data to a third country require a level of protection essentially equivalent to that in the Union; the importer's legal system must be assessed for access by public authorities.

entries.title: La Quadrature du Net and Others v Premier ministre and Others
entries.court: Court of Justice of the European Union
entries.principle: General and indiscriminate retention of traffic and location data is prohibited; targeted retention is permitted only to combat serious crime and terrorism, subject to strict safeguards.
entries.facts: A challenge to French data retention legislation.
entries.holding: General and indiscriminate retention of traffic and location data is prohibited; targeted retention is permitted only to combat serious crime and terrorism, subject to strict safeguards.
entries.judges: Court of Justice of the European Union

entries.title: Nubian Rights Forum & 2 others v Attorney General & 15 others
entries.court: High Court of Kenya (Constitutional and Human Rights Division)
entries.principle: A national biometric identification programme requires a clear statutory basis, a data protection impact assessment, safeguards against function creep and meaningful public participation before rollout; privacy limits must be necessary and proportionate.
entries.facts: The Nubian Rights Forum and others challenged the Huduma Namba (NIIMS) biometric registration programme. The petitioners alleged that the programme lacked a statutory basis, a data protection impact assessment and adequate safeguards. The case raised questions of privacy, data protection and public participation.
entries.holding: A national biometric identification programme requires a clear statutory basis, a data protection impact assessment, safeguards against function creep and meaningful public participation before rollout.

entries.title: R (Bridges) v Chief Constable of South Wales Police
entries.court: Court of Appeal of England and Wales
entries.principle: The use of automated facial recognition in public spaces engages Article 8 and must be necessary, proportionate and subject to an adequate legal framework.
entries.facts: A challenge to the use of automated facial recognition by the police.
entries.holding: The use of automated facial recognition in public spaces engages Article 8 and must be necessary, proportionate and subject to an adequate legal framework.
entries.judges: Sir Terence Etherton MR (Court of Appeal)

entries.title: R (Bridges) v Chief Constable of South Wales Police
entries.court: Court of Appeal of England and Wales
entries.principle: The use of automated facial recognition in public spaces engages Article 8 and must be necessary, proportionate and subject to an adequate legal framework.
entries.facts: A challenge to the use of automated facial recognition by the police.
entries.holding: The use of automated facial recognition in public spaces engages Article 8 and must be necessary, proportionate and subject to an adequate legal framework.
entries.judges: Court of Appeal of England and Wales

entries.title: R (Gaughran) v Chief Constable of the Police Service of Northern Ireland
entries.court: Supreme Court of the United Kingdom
entries.principle: The indefinite retention of biometric data of a person convicted of a minor offence, without review, is disproportionate and unlawful.
entries.facts: A challenge to the indefinite retention of biometric data of a person convicted of a minor offence.
entries.holding: The indefinite retention of biometric data of a person convicted of a minor offence, without review, is disproportionate and unlawful.

entries.title: Bundesverband der Verbraucherzentralen und Verbraucherverbände — Verbraucherzentrale Bundesverband eV v Planet49 GmbH
entries.court: Court of Justice of the European Union
entries.principle: Consent to the storage of cookies must be active, specific and informed; pre-ticked boxes do not constitute valid consent.
entries.facts: A challenge to the use of pre-ticked boxes for cookie consent.
entries.holding: Consent to the storage of cookies must be active, specific and informed; pre-ticked boxes do not constitute valid consent.
entries.judges: Court of Justice of the European Union

entries.title: Data Protection Act 2019
entries.citation: Data Protection Act 2019 (Kenya), sections 25–31, 32 and Part VI
entries.principle: Personal data must be processed lawfully, fairly and transparently, for specified purposes and no longer than necessary; sensitive categories attract stricter conditions; cross-border transfers require proof of appropriate safeguards.

entries.title: Fashion ID GmbH & Co KG v Verbraucherzentrale NRW eV
entries.court: Court of Justice of the European Union
entries.principle: A website operator that embeds a social plugin is a joint controller for the collection and transmission of visitors' personal data to the plugin provider.
entries.facts: A challenge to the embedding of a Facebook Like button on a website.
entries.holding: A website operator that embeds a social plugin is a joint controller for the collection and transmission of visitors' personal data to the plugin provider.
entries.judges: Court of Justice of the European Union

entries.title: Google LLC v Commission nationale de l'informatique et des libertés (CNIL)
entries.court: Court of Justice of the European Union
entries.principle: The right to be forgotten does not automatically require de-referencing on all versions of a search engine; the assessment is made on a case-by-case basis.
entries.facts: A request for global de-referencing of search results.
entries.holding: The right to be forgotten does not automatically require de-referencing on all versions of a search engine; the assessment is made on a case-by-case basis.
entries.judges: Court of Justice of the European Union

entries.title: López Ribalda and Others v Spain
entries.court: European Court of Human Rights (Grand Chamber)
entries.principle: Covert video surveillance of employees is a serious intrusion into private life; it must be justified by a legitimate aim and be proportionate, with adequate safeguards.
entries.facts: Employees were subjected to covert video surveillance at work.
entries.holding: Covert video surveillance of employees is a serious intrusion into private life; it must be justified by a legitimate aim and be proportionate, with adequate safeguards.
entries.judges: European Court of Human Rights (Grand Chamber)

entries.title: R (Privacy International) v Investigatory Powers Tribunal
entries.court: Supreme Court of the United Kingdom
entries.principle: Statutory ouster clauses are construed strictly; judicial review of the legality of surveillance is a constitutional safeguard that Parliament is presumed not to have removed without clear words.
entries.facts: A challenge to the Investigatory Powers Tribunal's decisions on surveillance.
entries.holding: Statutory ouster clauses are construed strictly; judicial review of the legality of surveillance is a constitutional safeguard that Parliament is presumed not to have removed without clear words.

entries.title: African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights v Republic of Kenya (Ogiek case)
entries.court: African Court on Human and Peoples' Rights
entries.principle: The eviction of the Ogiek from the Mau Forest without due process violated their rights to property, natural resources, culture, religion and non-discrimination under the Charter.

entries.title: Bărbulescu v Romania
entries.court: European Court of Human Rights (Grand Chamber)
entries.principle: The monitoring of an employee's electronic communications must be proportionate; the employer must provide adequate safeguards and the employee must be informed.
entries.facts: An employee was dismissed after his employer monitored his electronic communications.
entries.holding: The monitoring of an employee's electronic communications must be proportionate; the employer must provide adequate safeguards and the employee must be informed.
entries.judges: European Court of Human Rights (Grand Chamber)

entries.title: Joshua Rodney Marimbah v Kenya Revenue Authority
entries.court: Employment and Labour Relations Court of Kenya
entries.principle: The collection and use of personal data by an employer or public body must be lawful, necessary and proportionate; monitoring of employees must respect privacy.
entries.facts: An employee challenged the collection and use of his personal data by the Kenya Revenue Authority. The dispute concerned workplace monitoring and data protection. The case raised questions of privacy in employment.
entries.holding: The Court held that the collection and use of personal data must comply with data protection principles; excessive or unjustified monitoring violates the right to privacy.
entries.judges: M. Mbaru J (Employment and Labour Relations Court)

entries.title: Satakunnan Markkinapörssi Oy and Satamedia Oy v Finland
entries.principle: The publication of personal data must be balanced against the public interest in receiving the information, taking account of the sensitivity of the data and the availability of safeguards.

entries.title: General Data Protection Regulation (EU) 2016/679
entries.citation: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 of the European Parliament and of the Council [2016] OJ L119/1
entries.principle: Processing requires a lawful basis and respect for principles of minimisation, storage limitation and integrity; transfers outside the Union require an adequacy decision or appropriate safeguards.

entries.title: PJS v News Group Newspapers Ltd
entries.court: Supreme Court of the United Kingdom
entries.principle: An interim injunction restraining publication of private information should be refused only where the public-interest defence is likely to succeed, and the internet's ready availability does not by itself remove protection.
entries.facts: A newspaper sought to publish details of a celebrity's extramarital affair.
entries.holding: An interim injunction restraining publication of private information should be refused only where the public-interest defence is likely to succeed.

entries.title: Patrick Breyer v Bundesrepublik Deutschland
entries.court: Court of Justice of the European Union
entries.principle: A dynamic IP address constitutes personal data where the controller has legal means to identify the data subject with additional information held by the ISP.
entries.facts: A challenge to the retention of dynamic IP addresses by a German federal institution.
entries.holding: A dynamic IP address constitutes personal data where the controller has legal means to identify the data subject with additional information held by the ISP.
entries.judges: Court of Justice of the European Union

entries.title: Tele2 Sverige AB v Post- och telestyrelsen
entries.court: Court of Justice of the European Union
entries.principle: General and indiscriminate retention of traffic and location data is unlawful; access must be limited to serious crime, restricted to necessary data and subject to prior review.

entries.title: AIDS Law Project v Attorney General & Another
entries.principle: The collection and use of HIV status data must be lawful, necessary and proportionate; mandatory testing and disclosure of HIV status without consent violates the right to privacy and dignity.
entries.facts: The AIDS Law Project challenged provisions of the HIV and AIDS Prevention and Control Act that mandated HIV testing and disclosure of status. The petitioner argued that compulsory testing and disclosure violated the right to privacy and dignity. The case raised questions of bodily autonomy and medical confidentiality.
entries.holding: The Court held that mandatory HIV testing and disclosure of status without consent violated the right to privacy and dignity under Article 31 and Article 28 of the Constitution. The offending provisions were declared unconstitutional.

entries.title: J W I & Another v Standard Group Limited & Another
entries.principle: The publication of private information about a person's health status violates the right to privacy; the media must balance the public interest against the individual's right to privacy.
entries.facts: The petitioners challenged the publication of their HIV status and medical information by a newspaper. The publication disclosed their identities and health status without consent. The case raised questions of media freedom and the right to privacy.
entries.holding: The Court held that the publication violated the petitioners' right to privacy under Article 31 and awarded damages. The media's right to freedom of expression must be balanced against the individual's right to privacy, especially for sensitive health data.

entries.title: R (Catt) v Commissioner of Police of the Metropolis
entries.court: Supreme Court of the United Kingdom
entries.principle: The retention of personal data by the police must be justified by a pressing need and be proportionate; retention of data on non-violent protesters was unlawful.
entries.facts: A challenge to the retention of data on a peaceful protester.
entries.holding: The retention of personal data by the police must be justified by a pressing need and be proportionate; retention of data on non-violent protesters was unlawful.

entries.title: Vidal-Hall v Google Inc
entries.court: Court of Appeal of England and Wales
entries.principle: Damages for distress are available for breach of data protection law without proof of pecuniary loss.
entries.facts: A claim for damages for misuse of private information by Google.
entries.holding: Damages for distress are available for breach of data protection law without proof of pecuniary loss.

entries.title: Digital Rights Ireland Ltd v Minister for Communications, Marine and Natural Resources
entries.court: Court of Justice of the European Union
entries.principle: Blanket retention of communications data is disproportionate; data retention must be limited to what is strictly necessary and accompanied by adequate safeguards.

entries.title: Google Spain SL and Google Inc v Agencia Española de Protección de Datos (AEPD) and Mario Costeja González
entries.court: Court of Justice of the European Union
entries.principle: A search engine is a controller of personal data and may be required to remove links to information that is inadequate, irrelevant or excessive in relation to the purposes of processing.

entries.title: R (T) v Chief Constable of Greater Manchester Police
entries.court: Supreme Court of the United Kingdom
entries.principle: The blanket disclosure of minor, old or irrelevant convictions in enhanced criminal-record certificates is disproportionate and incompatible with Article 8.
entries.facts: A challenge to the blanket disclosure of minor, old or irrelevant convictions.
entries.holding: The blanket disclosure of minor, old or irrelevant convictions in enhanced criminal-record certificates is disproportionate and incompatible with Article 8.

entries.title: Bank Mellat v HM Treasury (No 2)
entries.court: Supreme Court of the United Kingdom
entries.principle: Proportionality asks whether the objective is sufficiently important, the measure is rationally connected to it, a less intrusive alternative exists, and the impact on rights is not disproportionate to the benefit.
entries.facts: The Treasury directed that an Iranian bank be excluded from the UK financial system.
entries.holding: Proportionality asks whether the objective is sufficiently important, the measure is rationally connected to it, a less intrusive alternative exists, and the impact on rights is not disproportionate to the benefit.

entries.title: Constitution of Kenya 2010
entries.principle: The Constitution is a living instrument: national values bind all State organs, rights are interpreted expansively, limitations must be reasonable and justifiable under Article 24, and the Supreme Court's advisory jurisdiction is exclusive.

entries.title: Uzun v Germany
entries.principle: The use of GPS tracking to monitor a suspect's movements engages Article 8; it must be necessary and proportionate to a legitimate aim.
entries.facts: A challenge to the use of GPS tracking to monitor a suspect.
entries.holding: The use of GPS tracking to monitor a suspect's movements engages Article 8; it must be necessary and proportionate to a legitimate aim.

entries.title: R (L) v Commissioner of Police of the Metropolis
entries.court: Supreme Court of the United Kingdom
entries.principle: The retention and disclosure of allegations of criminal conduct that did not result in conviction must be necessary and proportionate.
entries.facts: A challenge to the retention and disclosure of allegations that did not result in conviction.
entries.holding: The retention and disclosure of allegations of criminal conduct that did not result in conviction must be necessary and proportionate.

entries.title: R (Wood) v Commissioner of Police of the Metropolis
entries.court: Court of Appeal of England and Wales
entries.principle: The retention and dissemination of photographs taken during a peaceful protest can engage Article 8, and the police must show that retention is necessary and proportionate to a legitimate policing purpose.
entries.facts: The police photographed and retained images of a peaceful protester.
entries.holding: The retention and dissemination of photographs taken during a peaceful protest can engage Article 8, and the police must show that retention is necessary and proportionate.

entries.title: I v Finland
entries.principle: The disclosure of a patient's medical data by a health authority without consent violates Article 8; medical data is a special category entitled to enhanced protection.
entries.facts: A challenge to the disclosure of a patient's medical data.
entries.holding: The disclosure of a patient's medical data by a health authority without consent violates Article 8; medical data is a special category entitled to enhanced protection.

entries.title: S and Marper v United Kingdom
entries.court: European Court of Human Rights (Grand Chamber)
entries.principle: The indefinite retention of fingerprints and DNA of persons not convicted of an offence is disproportionate and violates Article 8, even where the data is used for crime prevention.

entries.title: Copland v United Kingdom
entries.principle: The monitoring of an employee's telephone, email and internet use engages Article 8 where the employee has a reasonable expectation of privacy.
entries.facts: A challenge to the monitoring of an employee's telephone, email and internet use.
entries.holding: The monitoring of an employee's telephone, email and internet use engages Article 8 where the employee has a reasonable expectation of privacy.

entries.title: Weber and Saravia v Germany
entries.principle: Strategic monitoring of telecommunications must be subject to adequate safeguards, including independent authorisation and oversight, to be compatible with Article 8.
entries.facts: A challenge to strategic monitoring of telecommunications in Germany.
entries.holding: Strategic monitoring of telecommunications must be subject to adequate safeguards, including independent authorisation and oversight, to be compatible with Article 8.

entries.title: A v Secretary of State for the Home Department
entries.principle: Indefinite detention of foreign nationals without trial was a disproportionate and discriminatory response to a public emergency, and deference does not extend to the choice of means that discriminate.
entries.facts: Foreign nationals were detained indefinitely without trial under anti-terrorism legislation.
entries.holding: Indefinite detention of foreign nationals without trial was a disproportionate and discriminatory response to a public emergency; deference does not extend to the choice of means that discriminate.

entries.title: Campbell v MGN Ltd
entries.principle: Misuse of private information is a distinct tort; where the information is private, the court balances the claimant's Article 8 rights against the publisher's Article 10 rights.
entries.facts: A newspaper published photographs and details of a model's drug addiction treatment.
entries.holding: Misuse of private information is a distinct tort; where the information is private, the court balances the claimant's Article 8 rights against the publisher's Article 10 rights.

entries.title: R (Daly) v Secretary of State for the Home Department
entries.principle: Where fundamental rights are engaged, the common law applies a proportionality test stricter than Wednesbury unreasonableness, asking whether the interference is necessary and no more than required.
entries.facts: A prisoner's legal correspondence was opened and read by prison officers.
entries.holding: Where fundamental rights are engaged, the common law applies a proportionality test stricter than Wednesbury unreasonableness, asking whether the interference is necessary and no more than required.

entries.title: Amann v Switzerland
entries.principle: The collection and storage of personal data by a public authority, even where not disclosed, engages Article 8 where the data is used to build a personal profile.

entries.title: Khan v United Kingdom
entries.principle: Covert surveillance that is not in accordance with law violates Article 8; the law must be accessible and foreseeable.
entries.facts: A challenge to covert surveillance by the police.
entries.holding: Covert surveillance that is not in accordance with law violates Article 8; the law must be accessible and foreseeable.

entries.title: Rotaru v Romania
entries.principle: The storage of personal data by a public authority engages Article 8 where the data is used to build a personal profile, even if not disclosed.
entries.facts: A challenge to the storage of personal data by the Romanian intelligence service.
entries.holding: The storage of personal data by a public authority engages Article 8 where the data is used to build a personal profile, even if not disclosed.

entries.title: Halford v United Kingdom
entries.principle: The interception of telephone calls on an office extension engages Article 8 where the employee has a reasonable expectation of privacy.
entries.facts: A senior police officer's telephone calls were intercepted.
entries.holding: The interception of telephone calls on an office extension engages Article 8 where the employee has a reasonable expectation of privacy.

entries.title: Z v Finland
entries.principle: Medical data is a special category of personal data entitled to enhanced protection; disclosure of such data requires compelling justification.

entries.title: Malone v United Kingdom
entries.principle: The interception of communications must be in accordance with law; a system that is not prescribed by law with sufficient precision violates Article 8.
entries.facts: A challenge to the interception of telephone communications in the UK.
entries.holding: The interception of communications must be in accordance with law; a system that is not prescribed by law with sufficient precision violates Article 8.

entries.title: African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights
entries.citation: African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights (adopted 27 June 1981, entered into force 21 October 1986) 1520 UNTS 217
entries.principle: States undertake to recognise and give effect to Charter rights without distinction, to guarantee independence of courts, and to ensure that remedies are available for violations.

entries.title: Klass and Others v Germany
entries.principle: Secret surveillance of communications is permissible only where it is in accordance with law, necessary in a democratic society and subject to adequate safeguards against abuse.
entries.facts: A challenge to secret surveillance of telecommunications in Germany.
entries.holding: Secret surveillance of communications is permissible only where it is in accordance with law, necessary in a democratic society and subject to adequate safeguards against abuse.

entries.title: International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights
entries.citation: International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (adopted 16 December 1966, entered into force 23 March 1976) 999 UNTS 171
entries.principle: No one shall be subjected to arbitrary or unlawful interference with privacy; restrictions on expression must be provided by law and necessary to protect a legitimate interest.

entries.title: European Convention on Human Rights
entries.citation: Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (as amended) ETS 5, articles 8 and 10
entries.principle: Interference with private life or expression must be prescribed by law and necessary in a democratic society for a legitimate aim, assessed through the proportionality and margin-of-appreciation analysis.

entries.title: Entick v Carrington
entries.principle: Executive interference with person or property requires positive legal authority; necessity of state is not a substitute for law, and every invasion of private right needs justification.
entries.facts: The King's messengers entered Entick's house and seized his papers under a warrant issued by the Secretary of State.
entries.holding: Executive interference with person or property requires positive legal authority; necessity of state is not a substitute for law.
entries.judges: Lord Camden CJ (Court of King's Bench)

entries.title: African Union Convention on Cyber Security and Personal Data Protection
entries.principle: Regional benchmark for data protection in African moots.
entries.note: Regional benchmark for data protection in African moots.

entries.title: Convention 108+ (Council of Europe Convention on the Protection of Individuals with regard to Automatic Processing of Personal Data)
entries.principle: International benchmark for data protection, relied on in privacy moots.
entries.note: International benchmark for data protection, relied on in privacy moots.

entries.title: Data Protection (General) Regulations, 2021
entries.principle: Consent, processing principles, controller–processor contracts (reg 24) and cross-border transfers (reg 41).
entries.note: Consent, processing principles, controller–processor contracts (reg 24) and cross-border transfers (reg 41).

entries.title: Data Protection (Registration of Data Controllers and Data Processors) Regulations, 2021
entries.principle: Registration regime and the framework within which the ODPC's enforcement powers are exercised.
entries.note: Registration regime and the framework within which the ODPC's enforcement powers are exercised.

entries.title: Data Protection Act, 2019
entries.principle: The primary instrument for ODPC and privacy moots: principles (ss 25–31), consent, DPIA (s 31), data subject rights and Part VI (cross-border transfers).
entries.note: The primary instrument for ODPC and privacy moots: principles (ss 25–31), consent, DPIA (s 31), data subject rights and Part VI (cross-border transfers).

entries.title: European Data Protection Board Guidelines
entries.citation: EDPB Guidelines 05/2021 (interplay between Article 3 and Chapter V GDPR)
entries.principle: Authoritative guidance on cross-border transfers and extraterritorial application.
entries.note: Authoritative guidance on cross-border transfers and extraterritorial application.

entries.title: General Data Protection Regulation (EU) 2016/679
entries.principle: Benchmark for lawful bases, transfers and accountability.
entries.note: Benchmark for lawful bases, transfers and accountability.

entries.title: International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights
entries.principle: Articles 17 (privacy) and 19 (expression) are the workhorses of rights-based moots.
entries.note: Articles 17 (privacy) and 19 (expression) are the workhorses of rights-based moots.

entries.title: Office of the Data Protection Commissioner (Kenya)
entries.principle: DPIA, consent and education-sector guidance; the regulator's own view of the Act.
entries.note: DPIA, consent and education-sector guidance; the regulator's own view of the Act.
